claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A physics-informed machine-learning model using hierarchical microstructural descriptors can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness for HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed model will be more efficient than first-principles and CALPHAD methods.
The proposed model will be more accurate than first-principles and CALPHAD methods.
Local chemical fluctuations and grain-boundary distributions can serve as coarse-grained descriptors of the hierarchical structure.
The model will be trained using combined experimental and simulation data from tensile and fracture testing.
The intended prediction regime is room temperature while the hierarchical heterostructure remains stable.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and grain-boundary distributions mediate elastic deformation behavior.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and grain-boundary distributions mediate crack initiation and propagation.
Embedding physical constraints in the machine-learning architecture filters nonphysical correlations.
Embedding physical constraints enables accurate representation of microstructure–property relationships.
The physics-informed model reduces reliance on computationally costly simulations.
The model is expected to reduce computational demands by approximately tenfold relative to conventional methods.
The model is expected to reduce prediction error for tensile and fracture properties by approximately 50% relative to conventional methods.
First-principles, CALPHAD, and standard machine-learning approaches are computationally intensive and have comparatively large predictive uncertainties, especially for fracture toughness.
The model may cease to be reliable when high temperature, irradiation, or out-of-training-regime composition changes significantly alter the hierarchical heterostructure.
A blinded prospective benchmark will use new HfNbTiVAl10 samples retaining the hierarchical heterostructure and will compare preregistered predictions against tensile and fracture measurements.
The hypothesis will be deemed falsified if predictions differ from experiment by more than 10% for at least two of the three properties or if computational cost is reduced by less than tenfold.
